papers.title: Atmospheric pollution contributed to destabilizing a small mammal community amid four decades of environmental changes
papers.abstract: In the recent decades, climatic and land-use changes paralleled major decreases in atmospheric pollution, but unclear is how these concomitant changes shape ecological dynamics. We analyzed 39 years (1986-2024) of semiannual abundances for six small-mammal species in the Black Triangle of Europe (Czechia), a region historically-marked by acidic rains causing forest diebacks and toxic lead (Pb) deposition. We combined these small-mammal data with monthly time series of atmospheric pollution, vegetation index (NDVI), meteorology and soil moisture. We used Empirical Dynamic Modelling (EDM) to infer chaos, recover species-species and environment-species causal relationships, recover time-varying interactions, and perform out-of-sample forecasts. Small mammal populations were causally affected by atmospheric pollution, and its abrupt decline in the late 1990s likely triggered a delayed critical transition of community composition. Pollution primarily affected the dominant omnivores and strengthened the interactions among species, a hallmark of instability. We identified a second route to chaos with a role of vegetation dynamics and soil moisture that was especially strong on shrews. Our feedback-loop analysis suggests how pollution and other environmental changes favored destabilizing, positive feedbacks. Forecasting of these chaotic dynamics improved when adding the relevant environmental predictors, demonstrating that the unpredictability of chaotic systems can slightly improve when we identify the main drivers of interactions in a network, offering hope for anticipating the future of complex ecosystems. Our study offers a unique retrospective of the destabilizing effects of pollution, an overlooked macro-ecological driver.

papers.title: Algal turf sediment dynamics across the Florida Reef Tract
papers.abstract: Algal turfs and their associated sediments are dominant components of many degraded reefs, where they mediate key ecosystem processes. However, the quantification of algal turfs and their sediments across reef shelves is limited outside Indo-Pacific reef systems. We quantified algal turf length, sediment loads, and sediment grain size distribution across four reef positions (nearshore, inner, middle, and outer) at three locations along the northern Florida Reef Tract (FRT). Sediment loads were positively associated with algal turf length and generally declined moving offshore. Nearshore reefs supported algal turfs that were both 1.6-fold longer and contained 1.6-fold higher sediment loads than on outer reefs, while sediment composition shifted toward finer grain sizes offshore. Nevertheless, regardless of reef position, all algal turfs had high sediment loads ranging from 1,445 to 16,639 g m-2. Our findings suggest that cross-shelf patterns in algal turf sediment dynamics are present on Western Atlantic reefs and reveal that long sediment-laden algal turfs dominate on the FRT. These results highlight the pervasive nature of sediment-laden algal turfs on degraded reefs and emphasize the need to monitor and manage their expansion on reefs subject to chronic coastal development and climate-driven disturbance.

papers.title: Plant-plant communication in tomato: mechanisms underpinning information transfer between plants
papers.abstract: As evidences about plant-plant communication are mounting, we lack a mechanistic understanding of intricate events occurring inside and among pairs of plants. This is needed to untangle proximal causes explaining how volatiles emitted by herbivore-attacked plants can enhance plant defence in intact neighbouring plant. A comprehensive knowledge of these interactions may favour their integration in trait-based agroecological frameworks. Based on an original experiment set-up, we connected infested sender plants and intact receiver plants during 3 days. We monitored metabolomic reprogramming of sender plant and progressive adjustments in their volatile emissions. Plant-plant communication was tested according to metabolomic priming of receiver plant. Information transfer was tracked with kinetics of volatile profiles and chemodiversity metrics grounded in information theory. Our results show that sender plants infested with Phtorimae absoluta undergo deep reconfiguration of immune systems and balance their emissions of mono- and sesquiterpenoids over 3 days. These changes in airborne cues result in similar reprograming of immune system in receiver plants. Additionally, we observed herbivory-driven relationships between chemodiversity of volatile profiles produced by sender and receiver plants. Both metabolome and volatilome suggest that plant-plant communication operates as mirror effects with receiver plants matching up their defences on that of sender plants. From an adaptative standpoint, this supports the idea that information conveyed among plants is explicit enough to warn receiver plant against appropriate stress. More generally, this study points that information transfer could rely not only on composition but also on chemodiversity of volatile cues. We discuss implications related to cue detection at the molecular scale and cue propagation at the plant cover scale. Bridging composition and chemodiversity of volatile cues opens interesting avenues to study the efficiency of communication system in noisy environments.

papers.title: Seeing danger? Visual constraints and collision risk in the Bearded Vulture Gypaetus barbatus
papers.abstract: The Bearded Vulture, Gypaetus barbatus is highly vulnerable to collisions with human-made aerial infrastructures. Yet, its visual sensory system remains poorly understood, limiting the development of species-specific collision mitigation measures. To address this gap, we characterized its visual ecology across four complementary dimensions: visual fields, spatial resolution, contrast sensitivity and spectral sensitivity of cone visual rhodopsins. Bearded vultures have no blind area in the direction of travel during foraging flight, indicating that frontal visual-field limitations are unlikely to contribute to their risk of collisions. Their axial length predicts high spatial visual resolution, suggesting that insufficient spatial resolution is unlikely to be a primary cause of collisions. By contrast, Bearded Vultures display very low peak contrast sensitivity compared to other birds, which may limit their ability to detect objects when contrast with the background, or within the objects themselves, is low. Functional characterization of the four cone visual pigments indicated sensitivity spanning approximately 350-640 nm, with a potential chromatic-discrimination range from 400 to 602 nm. Together, these results identify that contrast sensitivity, rather than visual-field configuration or spatial resolution, is a key perceptual constraint to consider in collision mitigation of the Bearded Vulture. Visual markers should therefore maximize both internal contrast and brightness contrast against the surrounding environment. More broadly, our multidisciplinary approach highlights how birds differ substantially in how they perceive anthropogenic structures and illustrates the importance of incorporating species-specific sensory ecology into conservation efforts, especially in the design of collision-mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Joint effects of climate change and urbanization accelerate plant biodiversity loss across urban green spaces
papers.abstract: Urbanization and climate change are rapidly reshaping biodiversity worldwide, yet their combined impacts on ecosystems remain poorly understood. Urban green spaces (UGS) underpin urban biodiversity, but differ widely in their structure, management, and exposure to global change. Here, we examine how these two drivers jointly influence plant communities across five major UGS types (allotments, private gardens, residential green spaces, parks, and ruderal areas) in three socio-culturally distinct Swiss cities. By combining vegetation surveys from 180 sites (60 sites per city) with species-specific thermal niches, high-resolution projections of historical and future urban microclimates, and land-use change scenarios, we trace how climate-driven species loss interacts with the shifting availability of urban habitats to shape biodiversity outcomes by mid-century. We found that UGS types differed markedly in their contributions to biodiversity, with allotments and ruderal areas supporting disproportionately high compositional uniqueness. However, climate change alone was projected to drive substantial plant diversity declines across all UGS types, with 40-80% of species exceeding their thermal niches by mid-century based on climate change scenario and UGS type. Although allotments exhibited relatively greater tolerance due to broader community-level thermal preferences, this advantage was undermined by their rapid decline under urbanization. When considered jointly, climate change and urbanization generated widespread biodiversity losses through complementary mechanisms: climate change drove species declines, while urbanization amplified these losses by disproportionately reducing high-value habitats. These results reveal a consistent trajectory of biodiversity decline across urban landscapes and highlight the need to conserve high-diversity yet shrinking UGS, particularly allotments, while enhancing the ecological value and climate resilience of expanding UGS, such as parks and residential areas, to safeguard future urban biodiversity under global change.

papers.title: Ecology of gene drives: Organism fitness under larval competition determines gene drive performance
papers.abstract: Gene drives are a promising technology to control disease vectors, such as mosquitoes. However, as these interventions aim to modify and/or control the population of disease vectors, a full understanding of how gene drives interact with the ecology of the target species is essential. In this study, we explore how larval competition determines gene drive performance. We first extend an agent-based model of the larval behaviour of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to obtain detailed predictions for gene drive designs under realistic larval competition. Using Bayesian optimisation techniques, we explore the performance of different gene drive designs and find the Pareto frontier of optimal underdominant drives with different release thresholds. To understand what determines the structure of the Pareto frontier, we conduct both local and global sensitivity analyses to assess the role different parameters play in determining gene drive performance. We find that ecological parameters, which determine the behaviour of the organism, dominate over genetic parameters for much of the parameter space, although genetic parameters play an important role at the frontier. Finally, we develop stochastic and deterministic surrogate models to enable efficient comparison and simulation without imposing the computational costs of agent-based approaches.

papers.title: A workflow to gather, clean, and standardize species occurrence records at scale for conservation applications
papers.abstract: Biodiversity declines and pressing threats to wildlife necessitate data-driven approaches for conservation and management planning. Natural resource agencies, conservation practitioners, and researchers increasingly leverage digital species occurrence records. However, we still lack user-friendly and flexible tools to aggregate, clean, and standardize such data. These tools are particularly needed for speciose groups like invertebrates and plants whose natural histories are poorly or unevenly known. To provide such a tool and overcome limitations of existing options, we developed a workflow in R that encompasses the entire process of aggregating, cleaning, and standardizing occurrence records within one free software platform. It additionally can return information useful for assessing species' conservation status. Key features include user friendliness, flexibility in data sources and filtering, handling large volumes of data or multiple species, and high transparency. We demonstrate workflow functionality focusing on Texas native bees. We combined bee data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) and several smaller datasets, then cleaned and standardized the combined dataset including removing duplicates. Processing 145,870 bee records took about an hour on a standard-configuration government computer. We used the resulting records in three case studies that demonstrated various uses conservation practitioners commonly implement. Case study 1 compiled a species list for Denton County, the second described phenology of bumble bees (Bombus genus) in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, and the third assessed conservation status of Bombus pensylvanicus. Our workflow greatly facilitates addressing a range of questions at various spatial and temporal scales from one vetted dataset that are tailored to the needs of a specific research objective, management question, municipality, or audience.

papers.title: Habitat degradation destabilizes complex metacommunities by disrupting dispersal
papers.abstract: Habitat loss and fragmentation are rapidly reshaping ecosystems worldwide, yet their consequences for ecological stability remain unresolved. Classical theory, pioneered by Robert May, established rigorous criteria for stability; however, these apply to spatially well-mixed communities, limiting their relevance to habitat degradation. Here, we develop a metacommunity framework that integrates classical stability theory with spatial dynamics to determine how anthropogenic habitat degradation reshapes ecosystem stability. We show that metacommunities exhibit three distinct dynamical regimes following a perturbation (e.g., drought or forest fire): stable regime (perturbations decay and species persist), reactive regime (perturbations are transiently amplified, which increases extinction risk under repeated disturbances), and unstable regime (perturbations grow, causing extinctions even after a single disturbance). Dispersal fundamentally reshapes these stability transitions, converting unstable communities into reactive ones and reactive communities into stable ones. While homogeneous dispersal progressively stabilizes communities, heterogeneous dispersal maximizes stability at intermediate strengths. We further show that habitat loss and fragmentation can be comparably effective at driving species extinctions by shifting metacommunities from stable to reactive and ultimately unstable regimes, demonstrating that fragmentation per se can be as important as habitat loss. Our findings reveal that reactivity is both an early-warning signal of impending instability and a state of elevated extinction risk under recurrent disturbances. By linking stability transitions to changes in population persistence under nonlinear dynamics, our results bridge classical stability theory with spatial ecology and provide a general framework for predicting how ecological complexity and dispersal jointly govern both ecosystem stability and population persistence under habitat degradation.

papers.title: Predicting seabird-vessel interactions from bird-borne data alone
papers.abstract: Seabirds often follow fishing vessels to scavenge discards and bait, benefiting from access to food but also facing the risk of bycatch. Exposure to bycatch is commonly assessed by analysing seabird-fishing interactions, typically through the spatiotemporal alignment of seabird and vessel tracking data. However, this approach may underestimate interactions when vessel tracking information is incomplete or unavailable. We tested whether seabird-vessel interactions could be identified using seabird telemetry alone and whether fishing and nonfishing vessels could be distinguished. We analysed GPS, wet-dry, accelerometer and pressure data from 273 Scopoli's shearwaters in the Northwest Mediterranean. We identified 779 vessel-attendance events using seabird GPS, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and simulation-based tests to distinguish vessel attraction or following from chance encounters. We then trained random forest models to predict vessel-attendance from bird-borne movement and environmental metrics, testing different sensor combinations. Finally, we selected the GPS and environmental model for its performance and compatibility with GPS-only tracking data from 17 radar-equipped shearwaters, whose detectors identified nearby vessels independently of AIS. Models predicting vessel-attendance from seabird movement metrics derived from GPS, wet-dry sensors and accelerometers achieved classification rates above 90% during training. However, when tested on new individuals, 42% of their positive predictions were false-positives. Models combining environmental metrics with either GPS or GPS and wet-dry data achieved classification rates around 75% during training and generalised consistently across individuals, maintaining classification rates of 70% or above. Attendance events involving fishing (n = 482) and nonfishing vessels (n = 297) could not be reliably distinguished. Across 45 trips of radar-equipped shearwaters, the GPS and environmental model discriminated vessel-attendance in hourly bins against AIS detections (AUC = 0.85), supporting assessment of spatiotemporal attendance patterns. At the event level, only 17% of 227 predicted vessel-attendance events were supported by AIS or radar detections. However, radar detected nearby vessels during 19 predicted events lacking AIS support, highlighting the value of complementary vessel detection. This study presents a vessel-independent framework for assessing seabird-vessel interactions based solely on bird-borne data, complementing fisheries monitoring programmes, helping to identify gaps in vessel-tracking systems across poorly monitored marine regions, and informing future assessments of bycatch risk.

papers.title: Long-term biodiversity responses to anthropogenic change are spatially and taxonomically heterogeneous across coastal wetlands
papers.abstract: Coastal wetlands have undergone centuries of anthropogenic modification, yet their long-term biodiversity trajectories remain poorly understood because ecological monitoring rarely extends beyond recent decades. Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) offers a historical perspective for evaluating how biodiversity patterns vary across environmental contexts and timescales. We combined COI and 18S sedaDNA metabarcoding with 210Pb and radiocarbon chronologies, sediment geochemistry and stable-isotope records from eight coastal wetlands across four regions of the Iberian Peninsula. We reconstructed changes in eukaryotic amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness and taxonomic composition and examined their relationships with an Anthropogenic Enrichment Index (AEI) based on ten elements potentially associated with human activities. Richness-AEI relationships differed among sediment records and genetic markers. Higher enrichment was associated with lower richness for both markers in one Cadiz record, whereas COI richness increased with enrichment in the Ebro Delta. However, after accounting for calendar time, only the positive association in the Ebro Delta remained statistically significant, indicating that several initial relationships were partly explained by shared temporal trends. Exploratory rolling correlations further suggested that the direction of richness-enrichment associations varied across historical periods within individual records. Taxonomic profiles differed between markers and wetlands, while community composition was strongly differentiated among sediment records, highlighting ecological variation not captured by richness alone. Multiproxy changes also followed locally specific configurations rather than a common regional trajectory. Together, these findings show that long-term relationships between sedimentary enrichment and biodiversity are context-dependent and sensitive to the temporal perspective considered. Integrating molecular, geochemical and isotopic records can therefore improve the historical interpretation of biodiversity change and inform conservation approaches that account for taxonomic composition, environmental history and locally appropriate reference conditions.

papers.title: The ecological niche and seasonality of Theileria equi in Portugal
papers.abstract: Equine piroplasmosis, caused by the tick-borne protozoan Theileria equi, is an evolving concern in Europe. In recent years, it has been associated with substantial economic costs and with transmission showing signs of pushing into previously free or marginal northern regions. While piroplasmosis is endemic in Portugal, not much is known about the interplay of seasonally varying and spatial abiotic drivers that may modulate infection. In this study, we leveraged unique field-surveillance data based on equine PCR testing together with publicly available data to unravel and characterize the spatio-temporal dynamics and ecological niche of Theileria equi. Infection probability was estimated to increase with local bovine abundance, temperature and the presence of planosol soils, and to decrease with local equine density due to an intraspecific dilution effect of vector exposure. At an individual level, the highest infection probabilities were estimated among female and pasture-kept equids. We estimate strong seasonal signatures in local and national infection probability, maximized in August and minimized in February, and a spatially heterogeneous ecological niche landscape. Far northern and north-eastern regions combined low infection probability both in- and off-season with prolonged off-seasons, whereas centre and north-western regions combined high probability both in- and off-season with brief off-seasons. The former plausibly function as unsuitable reservoirs, and the latter as suitable year-round reservoirs. Our results provide a first quantitative, risk-stratified basis for regional and individual targeted Theileria equi surveillance, awareness and control in Portugal.

papers.title: Species identity rather than colony size partitions shape variation in six Caribbean octocorals
papers.abstract: Caribbean reefs are increasingly dominated by arborescent octocorals as scleractinian cover declines. The physical structure of these octocoral forests is established by the manner in which octocoral species generate and modify colony form as they grow. We tested whether colony shape exhibited species-specific architecture and whether it changed allometrically with size. Two-dimensional projections of colony form were modeled as a series of stacked bands, whose areas were measured from scaled in situ images of colonies of six sympatric Caribbean octocorals from St John, US Virgin Islands. Principal component analysis (PCA) of relative band areas resolved a single dominant axis, accounting for 67.9% of the variation, that separated top-heavy from bottom-heavy colony profiles. Species identity explained 42% of the total variation in relative form, whereas colony height only explained 2% and had no detectable effect on either PCA axis. The proportion of the colony outline occupied by branches increased with height, from a predicted 41% at 20 cm to 52% at 100 cm. Colonies therefore grew without a detectable redistribution of area along their vertical axis, filling a species-specific outline more densely rather than moving along a common allometric trajectory. The vertical geometry of an octocoral canopy may therefore depend more on which species are present than on the sizes its colonies have reached.

papers.title: Intraspecific trait variation shapes macro-scale patterns ofniche breadth and range size
papers.abstract: Morphological variation within species may promote adaptation across ecological and geographic space, perhaps reflecting evolutionary plasticity and adaptability. Based on this concept, species with greater intraspecific variation in morphological traits may be expected to occupy broader ecological niches and larger geographic ranges. However, even in the age of global trait datasets, intraspecific morphological variation remains poorly quantified at broad taxonomic and geographic scales, limiting our understanding of how trait flexibility shapes ecological and biogeographic patterns. Focusing on 161 species of bulbuls, a widespread avian family containing some of the most abundant bird species in the world, along with some of the rarest and most restricted in range, we conducted global-scale sampling of morphological traits. These included beak shape, tarsus length and wing length, associated with dietary niche, foraging strategy and dispersal, respectively. Using phylogenetic models, we tested whether ecological niche breadth and geographical range size are predicted by intraspecific morphological variation quantified from 8,251 museum specimens and 5,627 live captures. Our results demonstrate that morphological trait variation predicts both ecological niche breadth and geographic range size. Furthermore, widespread species exhibit greater morphological variation than restricted-range species even when comparisons are constrained to equivalent geographic extents, consistent with the hypothesis that intraspecific trait variation facilitates range expansion rather than simply accumulating as a consequence of occupying a larger range. These results identify intraspecific morphological variation as a potentially important, yet largely overlooked, predictor of ecological traits and biogeographic distributions in birds.

papers.title: Particle-based representation of phytoplankton modulates emergent coexistence and biogeography in a model ocean
papers.abstract: Phytoplankton communities sustain the marine food web through primary productivity. These communities sustain a high diversity of species, all of which must draw from the same finite nutrient supply. The mechanisms driving phytoplankton biogeography and succession, as well as those enabling high diversity, remain incompletely understood. Here, we compare emerging patterns of biogeography, richness, and diversity in a size-structured phytoplankton community as it is advected and diffused within an idealized North Atlantic double-gyre circulation, using both Eulerian and Lagrangian (particle-based) modeling (PBM) frameworks. When a sufficient number of particles is modeled, the PBM, which resolves mortality at the particle level, produces stronger seasonal variability in biomass in the northern gyre and less stable and higher biomass in the southern gyre, while reproducing large-scale chlorophyll patterns observed by satellite. These contrasting dynamics are accompanied by distinct regional diversity patterns: local richness and diversity are generally higher in the PBM than in the Eulerian model in the northern gyre, with differences depending on the mortality threshold, whereas in the oligotrophic southern gyre, PBM local richness increases with particle number, while Eulerian richness is more sensitive to the mortality threshold. The PBM also produces a dynamic and emergent biogeographical structure that is more robust to the mortality threshold than the Eulerian model. Finally, Lagrangian variability in environmental conditions experienced by particles shows a stronger impact compared to the local Eulerian variability in the Northern gyre and stresses variable sensitivity to environmental histories. Together, these results suggest that the discrete representation of biomass fundamentally alters mortality, biogeography, and emergent coexistence patterns in model plankton ecosystems.

papers.title: Interactive effects of Nutrient Enrichment and Water Scarcity on Floral signaling and visitation
papers.abstract: - Floral traits remain an underexplored frontier in global change biology compared to their vegetative counterparts. As anthropogenic change involves simultaneous shifts in resource availability, focusing on isolated stressors may overlook complex biological responses. Characterizing the interactive effects of these stressors is therefore crucial to move beyond additive models and accurately predict the stability of pollination services in a transforming world. - The individual and interactive effects of nutrient enrichment and water scarcity were investigated on the floral traits and pollinator visitation rates of five grassland species. - While species identity emerged as the dominant driver of overall trait variation, across-species responses were also present. Among the abiotic drivers, nutrient enrichment emerged as the primary influence, significantly increasing flower number and achromatic contrast while decreasing floral area, chromatic contrast and chroma. Conversely, water scarcity primarily reduced plant height and increased floral chroma and hue. The two factors also often interacted in their effects. The changes in visual traits scaled up to changes in pollinator visitation, but the specific effects were largely species-specific. - Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that anthropogenic stressors act in divergent ways to reshape floral phenotypes and pollinator visitation, advancing our understanding of plant-pollinator interactions under compounding global pressures.

papers.title: Concrete waste as a source of calcium and alkalinity for coccolithophore cultivation: an experimental test of carbon dioxide removal and sequestration
papers.abstract: Cultivation of calcifying microalgae has been proposed as a route to carbon dioxide removal (CDR), but biogenic calcification releases CO2 unless the calcium supplied also adds alkalinity. We used cultures of the coccolithophore Chrysotila sp to test whether hydrated lime (Ca(OH)2), supplied as a reagent or within ground waste concrete, can provide both calcium and alkalinity. In a 26-day factorial batch experiment, we monitored pH, nitrate and dissolved calcium. Calcite was quantified by thermogravimetric analysis. Nitrate concentration decreased and calcite accumulated in all algal treatments, indicating that lime or concrete did not inhibit growth or calcification. Lime and concrete raised culture pH significantly whereas the algal growth rate inferred from nitrate drawdown did not differ among treatments. Calcite production was 3.6-fold higher with lime than in seawater (4.5 vs. 1.2 mg L-1 d-1) and highly variable with concrete; lime and concrete cultures remained supersaturated with respect to calcite ({Omega} {approx} 7-10 vs. 0.2). Carbonate-system calculations indicate that the added alkalinity raises the equilibrium CO2 uptake capacity of the medium by ca. 3.4 mmol kg-1, offsetting CO2 released by calcification. These results provide proof of concept for coupling coccolithophore cultivation with concrete waste reuse for CDR.

papers.title: Combined elevated temperature and CO2 alter Wolbachia abundance and host fitness but not cytoplasmic incompatibility in a stored-product pest
papers.abstract: Coinfecting endosymbiont strains may respond differently to environmental change, with consequences for host performance and reproductive incompatibility. We investigated an isofemale line of Callosobruchus chinensis coinfected with the cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI)-inducing Wolbachia strains wBruCon (Con) and wBruOri (Ori), together with derived Con-only and uninfected sublines. Beetles were maintained under control conditions (30{degrees}C, ~500 ppm CO2) or under combined elevated temperature and CO2 (32{degrees}C, ~1000 ppm CO2; eT&CO2). In coinfected adults, Ori relative abundance declined under eT&CO2, whereas Con abundance increased in females. Con responses also depended on host sex and infection status, with singly infected males showing particularly high abundance under control conditions. However, CI expression remained stable across environmental conditions. Coinfected females laid fewer eggs than uninfected females, whereas host life-history responses to eT&CO2 varied among traits and generations. eT&CO2 accelerated development and reduced adult longevity, while reduced egg-adult survival emerged in the F2 generation. It also reduced F1 fecundity but only in the uninfected subline. Strong and partial CI associated with Con and Ori, respectively, remained evident under both environmental conditions. Equilibrium analyses incorporating relative fecundity, CI intensity, and maternal transmission suggested lower infection persistence under eT&CO2 in the F1 generation but higher persistence in the F2 generation. Sensitivity analysis suggested contribution of improved relative fecundity of infected females in the latter. Overall, the two Wolbachia strains exhibited contrasting, sex-dependent abundance responses to eT&CO2, while CI expression remained stable. These findings suggest that climate change may alter symbiont infection dynamics in economically important pests, with potential implications for symbiont-mediated traits, including pesticide resistance.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Signatures Suggest Epigenetic Programming of Molecular Defense in Biochar-Exposed Formica japonica
papers.abstract: Previous transcriptomic analyses revealed that exposing the ant species Formica japonica to biochar induces a priming effect that is sustained under heavy metal stress and enhances the ants' resilience. Re-evaluation of the data shows that biochar exposure acts as an epigenetic switch, programming the ants' defense mechanisms and enhancing their resilience to various environmental stressors. Exposure to humic-like substances, such as biochar leachate, prepares insects to withstand not only heavy metals but also other environmental challenges, such as exposure to xenobiotics, pathogens, and parasites.

papers.title: Identifying the source population of naturally recolonised rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary, Assam, through multidisciplinary methods
papers.abstract: Megaherbivore population recovery largely depends on restoring connectivity between fragmented protected areas to facilitate natural dispersal, gene flow, and range expansion. The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) has recovered from severe population decline in the past, but several populations remain spatially restricted. Recent conservation efforts and the expansion of protected areas in Assam have coincided with natural rhino recolonization in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS). This has occurred from nearby regions of Orang NP and Kaziranga NP after the species was locally extinct in the 1980s. Identifying the source population of these recolonised rhinos is crucial for managing this emerging metapopulation. We used non-invasive genetic sampling, genetic assignment and a landscape connectivity model to investigate the origin and potential movement routes of the recolonising rhinos. We identified eight unique individuals from Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS and assigned them to the potential source population using Bayesian and frequency-based approaches against a reference dataset of 365 individual rhinos across the rhino-bearing areas of Assam. Habitat suitability was modelled using 161 spatially thinned presence points and eight environmental variables. We applied least-cost path (LCP) analysis to assess landscape resistance between protected area nodes. All eight recolonising rhinos were assigned to Orang NP with high Bayesian assignment probabilities (q = 0.97-0.99). The connectivity model identified two least-cost pathways, with the Orang NP-Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS linkage showing lower landscape friction than the Kaziranga NP linkage. These findings provide genetic evidence that the recolonisation occurred through natural dispersal, most likely from Orang NP, and indicate that recent landscape restoration has re-established the structural connectivity across this floodplain. Maintaining these linkages will be essential to promote natural range expansion and the long-term persistence of Indian rhinoceros in Assam.

papers.title: Tropical Peatlands as Hotspots of Hidden Arcellinida Diversity: Insights from Maludam National Park, Borneo (Sarawak, Malaysia)
papers.abstract: Recent investigations on tropical peatlands have shown their extremely high efficiency as carbon sinks, far beyond better studied boreal bogs. The microbial diversity found in those ecosystems, as well as their corresponding ecological and metabolic processes, are just starting to be revealed, and differ considerably from high latitudes systems. However, these efforts have been concentrated almost exclusively towards prokaryotes and fungi, leaving protist communities virtually unknown. Arcellinida (testate amoebae) are well acknowledged to play an important role in boreal and temperate peatland ecology by driving microbial community composition as top predators, but also as nutrient recyclers and carbon fixers. Yet, to our knowledge, no community-level study has addressed their diversity and its drivers in tropical peatlands. In this study, we surveyed Arcellinida communities' diversity across five functionally distinct vegetation-hydrological zones situated along a hydrological transect in a coastal tropical peatland in the Maludam National Park, Malaysia. Taxonomic composition of Arcellinida communities, characterized by a high diversity of Trigonopyxis-related taxa, indicated fundamental differences in diversity and community composition from extratropical ecosystems. Species richness was significantly higher in the zones with developed understory vegetation. Furthermore, the composition of diversity varied significantly among vegetation-hydrological zones. Altogether, this study shows unique Arcellinida communities in a Southeastern Asian peatland and suggests the importance of vegetation-hydrological characteristics for protist diversity.

papers.title: Harmonizing Repeated Multi-Platform Optical and LiDAR Observations for Continental-Scale Terrestrial Carbon Cycle Data Assimilation.
papers.abstract: Accurate monitoring of terrestrial carbon has attracted considerable attention due to the impacts of rapid climate change, disturbance, and land use on carbon storage and the growth of new global carbon markets and reporting requirements. While uncertainties in C estimates remain nontrivial, crucial opportunities exist to reduce uncertainty by rigorously harmonizing models and monitoring through data assimilation (DA). LiDAR has received considerable attention for its potential to inform carbon monitoring, and while there have been a number of papers on how to initialize models using LiDAR data, it has yet to be integrated into DA systems. In this study, we integrate GEDI LiDAR into an established DA system that already assimilates optical observations of aboveground biomass (AGB) and leaf area index (LAI), microwave soil moisture (SM), and ground-based soil organic carbon (SOC) to constrain C cycling processes across the entire North American continent. Notably, this is the first time both optical and LiDAR AGB products have been iteratively harmonized within a DA system. Results show that by assimilating both optical and LiDAR observations, we reduced the uncertainty in woody biomass by 63.7% relative to unconstrained model simulations and 18% relative to our previous DA system, and achieved an average RMSE reduction of 38.3 kg/m2 across five AGB products. Importantly, LiDAR reduces DA biases in high AGB regions where optical AGB estimates were exhibiting saturation. Analysis further identified the leading factors driving spatial error patterns within the DA system to be data quality, cloud coverage, and elevation. Overall, by bridging the spatial and temporal limitations of individual satellite products, this approach offers a practical, generalized workflow for high-resolution terrestrial carbon MRV in complex, dynamic ecosystems.

papers.title: Ancient environmental DNA reveals the distinct fingerprints of whaling and climate change on Antarctic marine biodiversity
papers.abstract: The Southern Ocean is a disproportionately large contributor to Earth system processes, playing a crucial role in the global transport of carbon, oxygen and heat. It also hosts enormous seasonal biological productivity that supports diverse endemic marine biodiversity. Industrial whaling in the first half of the 20th century and recent human-driven climate change have both profoundly altered Antarctic ecosystems, but ecological surveys of these impacts are limited to well-known taxa in the short period since monitoring began. Here, we analysed five sediment records to reconstruct more than two centuries of ecosystem change across the Western Antarctic Peninsula, spanning periods before and during major human impacts. Environmental DNA metabarcoding of these records revealed substantial biodiversity shifts, with change accelerating in recent decades. We find a significant role for both climate change and whaling in restructuring communities, identifying unique variance in whole-community change explained by each driver. Moreover, we find a negative association between whaling and metazoan families which feed from the water column, suggesting that pre-whaling ecosystems had greater pelagic productivity. Overall, our results reveal baseline Antarctic biodiversity from long before observational records and identify a distinct fingerprint of human drivers in this fragile, rapidly changing ecosystem.

papers.title: MillionTrees: A global benchmark for tree detection across geography, sensor, and annotation geometry
papers.abstract: Airborne tree monitoring using remotely sensed data, combined with the growth of computer vision models for object detection and segmentation, can facilitate broad scale assessment of tree health, ecology and ecosystem function. However, datasets for airborne tree detection have been largely limited to a single geography, resolution, or annotation approach, making it difficult to develop general models and benchmark their utility for broad applications. We compile existing and newly published annotation datasets to create a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating airborne tree detection in RGB imagery. The MillionTrees dataset has over a million individual trees from a broad range of forest types, tree species, and geographic locations. In addition, it has six million weakly supervised annotations from a range of sources including airborne LiDAR and photogrammetry, arborist surveys, and simulated landscapes. An evaluation standard is provided to facilitate rapid model development. We benchmark several existing tree detection algorithms and demonstrate that while current open-source models do not generalize across the diverse datasets in the benchmark, training on MillionTrees improves both within-domain and out-of-domain performance. Held-out validation datasets using ground truth derived from terrestrial LiDAR paired with overhead RGB show that overfitting to test data is common and hyperparameter tuning is an underappreciated challenge towards a global zero shot tree detection method. We discuss the limitations of the currently available data for airborne RGB tree detection, how to create more robust evaluation data and the need for better understanding of the uncertainty and utility of tree detection from airborne remote sensing.

papers.title: Optimal Conservation Prioritization for Waterfowl and Other Birds in Eastern Canada
papers.abstract: Conserving and restoring high-quality habitat is widely recognized as one of the most effective means of supporting migratory and wetland bird populations. To advance this objective at a regional scale, the Eastern Habitat Joint Venture (EHJV) coordinates conservation planning for 22 focal bird species across the eastern provinces of Canada. Optimization approaches to support conservation planning are increasingly common, and can be especially valuable in large areas where resources are limited. We present an optimized geospatial prioritization scheme designed to identify regions of primary importance to species coverage objectives within the EHJV. We apply linear programming methods to species abundance data products to maximize population coverage using an adaptable variable-target approach, whose outputs generalize readily to delivery projects of any budget or coverage goal. Our base results highlight areas of high conservation value for priority waterfowl and non-waterfowl species, and we present additional examples of how region-wide solutions can be subdivided based on jurisdictional boundaries, land ownership, or existing protected status. We also address methodological decision points, with attention to how available species abundance data sources were evaluated and what considerations were involved in formulating the optimization computations. We emphasize possibilities for future work to incorporate additional conservation values, such as carbon storage and flood mitigation, and costs, such as land value, and feasibility.

papers.title: Individual-specific recovery of the healthy human gut microbiota after antibiotics
papers.abstract: Following disruption by broad-spectrum antibiotics, the human gut microbiome undergoes a prolonged recovery where coarse ecological features, such as species richness and diversity, are largely restored. However, as these features are shared by most healthy individuals, it remains unclear whether, even after strong perturbation, individuals preferentially return toward their own pre-treatment composition ('individual-specific recovery') or instead switch to alternative equally healthy states. Resolving this question is fundamental for evaluating the long-term impacts of antibiotics, because an individual's health is affected by their unique microbiome composition, affecting immune regulation and metabolic processing, so a state switch, even to a broadly healthy configuration, could carry unintended consequences. Here we compare each subject's post-antibiotic endpoint with their own baseline and with the baselines of every other subject, across four cohorts (n = 121) whose regimens ranged from a five-day fluoroquinolone course to a four-day three-drug combination given to deplete the gut community. The recovered community was significantly closer to the subject's own baseline than to the alternative healthy baselines in more than 90% of individuals under the mildest regimen and in two thirds of those under regimens that broadly target the gut anaerobes, remaining above chance in every cohort and the majority outcome even where most baseline taxa fell below detection during treatment. This specificity is not merely the persistence and fast regrowth of survivors: it persists among baseline taxa that remain undetected for weeks to months, and the same taxon re-establishes more readily in a host where it was previously detected than in one where it was not. Newly established taxa are consistently more functionally similar to the pre-treatment community than transient arrivals, and their identity correlates with the surviving community's composition in a substantial fraction of subjects. State switching, in contrast, was uncommon and occurred almost exclusively among subjects with the largest reduction in detected taxa during the treatment. Together, these observations reveal the individual-specific nature of the microbiome resilience to broad-spectrum antibiotics, whereas the compositional changes are not random but rather functionally and ecologically associated with the subject's baseline.

papers.title: Enhancing Germination and Assessing the Longevity of Native Plants' Seeds with Dormancy through Different Priming Techniques
papers.abstract: Vachellia pachyceras and Convolvulus oxyphyllus are native species of arid and semi-arid desert regions, including Kuwait. They are inherently adapted to extreme conditions characterized by high temperature, prolonged drought and limited rainfall. They contribute significantly, to restore the ecosystem by providing food and shelter for wildlife. Despite their ecological importance, seed germination in both species is constrained by dormancy, and natural recruitment of seedlings is limited by narrow and unpredictable rainfall windows, severely restricting opportunities for establishment. In this context, seed priming is an effective pre-sowing technique that enables uniform and rapid germination within the short window of favorable conditions. This study aims to identify the optimal seed-priming techniques for these two keystone native species and to assess the effect of priming on seed longevity. The seeds were scarified to remove the physical dormancy prior to priming treatments. Relative seed longevity was measured for primed seeds through artificial ageing and analyzed using probit analysis and analysis of variance. Results showed that hormonal priming [(mechanical scarification + 100 ppm gibberellic acid (GA3)] for six hours and hydropriming (mechanical scarification + soaking in water) for 8 hours (h) were effective treatments among the tested priming treatments for V. pachyceras. The estimated p50 value (i.e., number of days to lose seed viability to 50%) was 22 days for hormonal priming and 21 days for hydropriming. Mechanical scarification followed by one and half hour of hydropriming was the most effective in C. oxyphyllus (p50 = 74 days). Based on these results, the longevity of V. pachyceras and C. oxyphyllus could be considered medium. Further studies are needed to determine the effectiveness of seed priming on additional ecologically and economically important native species to achieve success in revegetation programs.

papers.title: Validating static food web model diet matrices using stable isotope simulation
papers.abstract: End-to-end ecosystem models, such as Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE), are valuable tools for resource management. Within these frameworks, trophic interactions, typically derived from stomach contents analyses, govern system-wide energy flow via consumption. However, stomach contents data may be unrepresentative of long-term average diets and assimilated consumption due to factors including differential digestion rates and identifiability of prey, introducing model uncertainty. Because trophic interactions define model structure, variation in modeled diets can alter predictions and management conclusions. Consequently, evaluating and reducing uncertainty in diet matrix compositions is critical for operational acceptance of ecosystem models. Stable isotope analysis provides complementary, time-integrated insight into average diets, but its application for EwE validation has largely been limited to evaluating trophic levels and isotopic niche space. Here, we present a quantitative framework for simulating consumer stable isotope signatures across food webs from parent ecosystem models using a matrix-based mixing model. Using a published Northern Gulf of Mexico EwE model as a case study, we demonstrate Monte Carlo simulation to propagate uncertainty from basal source signatures and trophic discrimination factors. Comparison of predicted signatures with empirical {delta}13C and {delta}34S measurements enables validation of primary carbon sources and benthic-pelagic pathway contributions, revealing agreement in isotope space alongside mismatch in energy pathways. Diagnostic residuals identify discrepancies in diet composition. Model scoring provides a reproducible framework for ranking alternative diet configurations. Redundancy analysis further identifies within-group species coverage differences between stomach contents and isotope datasets as a primary driver of mismatch, highlighting an important consideration for sampling design.

papers.title: A mismatch in wildfire impact reduction and ecological restoration in western U.S. fuel treatments
papers.abstract: A century of fire suppression has made historically fire-adapted forests across the western U.S. denser and dominated by fire-intolerant trees, leading to severe fires. Fuel treatments aim to reduce wildfire impact and restore fire-adapted forests. Ecological theory suggests these objectives need not align: protecting the existing, fire-maladapted stand may prevent fire-tolerant seedling recruitment. Using Forest Inventory and Analysis data on 81,621 trees and 41,328 seedlings across 11 western U.S. states, we show that fuel treatments increase tree survival, but benefits are largest for fire-intolerant trees, fade within nine years, and come with no seedling composition shift towards fire-tolerant species. Concluding, fuel reduction reduces wildfire impacts but does not restore fire-adapted forests. Without changes in treatment design, long-term resilience will require repeated intervention.

papers.title: Hic sunt dracones: ancient DNA from the extinct palaeofauna of the tiny Mediterranean archipelago of Columbretes and its implications for human visitation
papers.abstract: The Columbretes archipelago in the Mediterranean is an example of deep isolation and sporadic human interaction during the Holocene. We recovered ancient DNA from 2,600-year-old microfauna and historical museum specimens to investigate the island's extinct fauna. Despite challenging preservation conditions, we successfully recovered mitogenomes from historical Vipera latastei specimens, and partial mitogenomes from snake, skink, and lizard subfossils. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the extinct Columbretes snake as Vipera latastei, sharing a haplotype with the historical specimen and clustering with modern populations from northeastern Iberia, validating its provenance and suggesting a single mitochondrial lineage since isolation. The extinct skink, Chalcides bedriagai, also shows affinities with eastern Iberia. These results point to a vicariant origin for the herpetofauna, likely isolated on the island following sea level rise after the Last Glacial Maximum. Conversely, a 2,600-year-old mouse incisor yielded a Mus musculus mitogenome, indicating Iron Age human-mediated introduction. Additionally, genomic analysis of a 11th-century CE human burial revealed an individual with genetic affinities to the Central Mediterranean and Balkans, highlighting medieval maritime mobility. This study resolves the long-debated Columbretes snake identity, traces biogeographic origins and illustrates the interplay of natural isolation and anthropogenic influence on the island biodiversity.

papers.title: Host specificity, seasonality, and urbanicity shape the gut microbiome of a synanthropic insect
papers.abstract: The soapberry bug Jadera haematoloma is a classic model of rapid adaptive evolution, with a well-documented host shift from native herbaceous sapinds to the introduced goldenrain tree (Koelreuteria spp.). This host shift has facilitated the insect's spread into novel anthropogenic urban habitats. Microbial associations are often critical to insect environmental adaptation. Here, we characterize the gut microbiota of J. haematoloma across native and introduced host plants, seasonal transitions, and a gradient of urbanicity. Our findings indicate that the soapberry bug gut microbiome is highly specialized, with a small number of core bacterial amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) primarily from the families Rhizobiaceae, Streptococcaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, and Lactobacillaceae. While traits such as sex and wing morph do not correlate with microbiome structure, the host plant acts as the primary determinant of community composition. Bugs feeding on the ancestral host plant maintain a more diverse and even microbial community featuring Enterobacteriaceae, whereas the gut environment of bugs on the introduced host is overwhelmingly dominated by a single unclassified Rhizobiaceae ASV. Furthermore, seasonal transitions drive significant turnover among accessory microbial taxa. Finally, we demonstrate that urbanization introduces a distinct ecological effect on the insect's microbiome. While the degree of local green space does not systematically alter within-host taxonomic richness, it is associated with modest change in mean community composition and significantly disrupts microbial community variance. Increased urbanization correlates with significantly higher beta dispersion, indicating that anthropogenic environments lead to more stochastic microbiomes, which may be an indicator of environmental stress. Together, these results illustrate how rapid dietary host shifts and the ecological pressures of urbanization interact to shape the microbiome of a synanthropic insect.
